`[[0] * 2] * 2` holds two references to the same row, so `g[1][1] = 2` changes both rows. `h` copies every row with `row[:]`, so the rows are separate objects, and `h[0][0] = 1` affects only the first row.

questions.prompt: What does `b = a[::-1]` do when a is a list?
options: Builds a new reversed list in O(n) time and O(n) space, and leaves a unchanged
Reverses a in place and also returns it
Returns a reversed view that shares memory with a
Reverses a in place and returns None
questions.explanation: A slice always creates a new list; the extended slice with step -1 walks backwards. Nothing is shared except the element references. In-place reversal is `a.reverse()` (returns None, O(n) time, O(1) space) and `reversed(a)` gives a lazy iterator.

questions.prompt: You must reverse a list in place with O(1) extra space. Which approach does that?
options: `a.reverse()`, or swap a[i] and a[n-1-i] with two pointers
`a = list(reversed(a))`
questions.explanation: `reverse()` and a two-pointer swap loop touch each element once with no new list: O(n) time, O(1) space. `a = a[::-1]` and `list(reversed(a))` build a new list and merely rebind the name, so callers holding the old list see no change. `a[:] = a[::-1]` does mutate the original but still allocates an O(n) temporary.
